in Google Docs, shared with
[Shambhala](shambala.qmd).

Dan Millman was a college gymnast, and the book is a semi-autobiographical
account of his apprenticeship to a gas-station attendant he calls Socrates. The
teaching arrives as instruction and correction during ordinary tasks rather than
as doctrine, and the warrior of the title is someone training in how to live
rather than someone preparing to fight.

## Concepts

- **There are no ordinary moments.** The claim the book turns on. Attention
  given to the current moment is the practice, and the search for a more
  significant one later is the obstacle.
- **Training covers body, mind and emotions together.** Fitness of one without
  the others leaves the whole unchanged.
- **Unreasonable happiness.** Satisfaction held independently of circumstances
  meeting your conditions, which removes the waiting.
- **A warrior acts; everyone else prepares to.** The test applied throughout is
  what was actually done, not what was understood.
